cluster_name: Australian World Cup footballer Volpato tests positive for cocaine
tldr: Nine of ten headlines reduce the Volpato incident to a single fact — a positive cocaine roadside test — with near-zero variation in framing across nine countries. The athlete's World Cup profile ('Socceroos star', 'World Cup star', 'Australian World Cup player') functions as the self-contained editorial justification for global pick-up; speeding mechanics appear in some headlines but the police encounter is never the lead. The institutional response — Football Australia's and the players' union's supportive holding statements — is entirely absent at the headline layer despite featuring in all full-text bodies, meaning the advertised story is both simpler and more sensational than what the texts report. The tenth item (The Telegraph) is a noise artifact: a 2025 celebrity-arrest headline sharing only the tokens 'star' and 'police' with the Volpato cluster.
event_summary: NSW police stopped Cristian Volpato, 22, for speeding on Sydney's Anzac Bridge at approximately 1:10 a.m. on July 24, 2026; a roadside drug test returned a positive result for cocaine.

single_outlet_findings.finding: The only cluster item unrelated to Volpato: a 2025 article about a Strictly Come Dancing celebrity arrested on suspicion of rape — a likely HDBSCAN noise inclusion on shared tokens ('star', 'police').

The only headline to frame the incident as an active investigation ('Australian footballer faces cocaine test probe') rather than an established fact. All other outlets assert the positive test directly; The Punch's 'probe' register introduces outcome uncertainty absent from the rest of the headline layer.

bottom_line: At the headline layer the Volpato cocaine test is an almost perfectly uniform CRIME_PUNISHMENT story: nine outlets in nine countries lead with the same police-drug-test allegation, with World Cup participation as the sole editorial justification for international pick-up. The gap with the body layer is significant — Football Australia's crisis management, union statements, and Italy's confirmatory-testing caveat are systematically absent from every headline, meaning the advertised story is both simpler and more sensational than what the full texts report.
